name: Pale Bluish Lavender
lede: Pale Bluish Lavender is a near-white grey-violet, built by putting the modifiers pale and bluish in front of the base color [[lavender]].

sections.title: Two modifiers on lavender
sections.body:
Pale Bluish Lavender stacks two modifier words, pale and bluish, in front of the base color [[lavender]], the compound-modifier grammar our library uses for names like this one [1]. It was first listed by Robert Ridgway in his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*, plate XXXVI, hue 57, tone f, and the Inter-Society Color Council later filed it in the ISCC-NBS 1955 system as block 213 (R) [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[languid-lavender]], only 3.1 units off, close enough on screen to read as the same pale violet [2]; [[pale-lilac]] and [[lavender-grey]] both sit within 4.2 units [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color within range of this swatch in 78 of 23,781 paintings, 0.33 percent, as photographed; looking for real coverage inside each painting narrows that to 51 [3]. That still makes it more common than half the named colors in our library [3]. It most often plays a light, in 84 percent of its 51 appearances by lightness rank, so varnish cannot fake the result [3]. John Singer Sargent is its most devoted painter, present in 7 of his 287 works here, 4.4 times the expected rate for the museums those paintings come from [3].

The earliest match dates to 1405, five hundred years before Ridgway's 1912 plate, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin; it marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a surviving pigment or dye [3].
